cards.name: Active voice
cards.summary: Make the doer the subject and put the action in the verb, so the reader knows who does what ('We processed your refund', not 'Your refund was processed'). Good active copy names the person or team responsible and keeps the sentence short.
use_for: service and product copy that promises an action ('Our team files your return')
emails and memos that assign tasks or ask for something
policy, scheme and government explainers where responsibility matters
help articles and instructions
apology and update emails that must own the problem
avoid: Forcing an actor in when it is unknown, obvious or unimportant ('The fort was built in 1726' is fine): keep the passive there.
Error messages that make the user the actor of a failure ('You entered an invalid PIN'): focus on the fix instead ('That PIN doesn't match. Try again or reset it').
Passive used to dodge blame in apologies and crisis statements ('Mistakes were made'): name who did it and what they are doing about it.
how: Find the passives: a form of 'be' (is, are, was, were, been, being, will be) followed by a past participle (reviewed, sent, approved), often with 'by ...'. In Hindi/Hinglish look for 'kiya gaya', 'bheja jayega'.
Ask who does the action. If the sentence has 'by X', move X to the front. If it has no actor, decide who it is (we, you, the bank, the committee) and name it.
Rewrite as actor + verb + object: 'Your documents will be verified by our team' becomes 'Our team verifies your documents'.
Prefer present or simple future tense after the switch; it usually shortens the sentence further.
Keep a passive only when you chose it: the actor is unknown or irrelevant, or the object is the real topic of the paragraph.
Re-read: if most sentences now start with 'We', rotate some to start with 'You' or the thing the reader cares about.
cards.before: The application will be reviewed by the committee and the decision will be communicated to you within 15 working days.
cards.after: The committee reviews your application and emails you its decision within 15 working days.
overuse_signs: Every sentence starts with 'We', so the copy is about the brand instead of the reader
Actors invented where none matters ('Somebody built this temple in 1600')
User-blaming error and warning messages
Method sections in academic or scientific writing rewritten against the house style that expects passive

cards.name: Alliteration
cards.summary: Repeat the same opening sound in two or three nearby stressed words so a headline, tagline or name is easier to say and remember. Good alliteration sounds natural and keeps the exact meaning; the sound is a bonus, never the reason for a word.
use_for: taglines and campaign lines
brand, product, series and segment names ('Monday Money Minute')
headlines, subheads and reel on-screen text
Hindi and Hinglish slogans where the sound carries ('Kam kharch, kamaal kaam')
avoid: Serious or sensitive copy (condolence notes, crisis statements, medical risk): sound play reads as flippant; write plainly.
Body copy: alliteration in every sentence turns prose into a jingle; keep it for one line per piece.
Swapping in a weaker or vaguer word to fit the sound ('fabulous finance' for a specific claim): meaning first, sound second.
how: Write the line plainly first, with the exact meaning you need.
List synonyms for the two or three key words and look for ones that share an opening SOUND (not letter: 'cheap chai' alliterates, 'city cake' does not).
Put the matching sounds on stressed words, adjacent or one word apart.
Stop at two or three words; four or more becomes a tongue-twister.
Read it aloud once; if the meaning bent to fit the sound, go back to the plain version.
For Hindi/Hinglish lines, alliterate on the Hindi sound the listener hears ('Pakka paisa, poori planning').
cards.before: Healthy home-style lunches delivered to offices in Pune.
cards.after: Dal, dabba, done: home-style lunch at your Pune desk by 1 pm.
overuse_signs: More than one alliterative line in a short piece
Four or more words in a row with the same sound
A word that only exists for the sound
Alliteration, rhyme and a pun stacked in the same line

cards.name: Anaphora and deliberate repetition
cards.summary: Start (anaphora) or end (epistrophe) several successive lines with the same words, so the repeated phrase builds rhythm and the changing part stands out. It works when the repeated phrase carries the point and the lines escalate.
use_for: speech climaxes and closes (keynote, political, wedding speeches)
brand manifestos and campaign films
reel and video voice-over lines cut to a beat
the turn of a LinkedIn post or op-ed
avoid: Short transactional copy (UX, search ads, SMS): repetition wastes a tight character budget; use a list.
More than one repetition run per piece: each one weakens the others; save it for the peak.
Repeating a vague phrase ('We believe...', 'We are...'): repetition amplifies weakness; repeat a concrete one.
how: Pick the phrase that holds your argument: a promise, a refrain or a 'for whom' (2-5 words).
Write three lines (four at most) that begin with it; keep it word-for-word identical and vary only what follows.
Order the lines from smallest to largest stake so the last one lands hardest.
Make the varying part concrete: a person, a number, a place.
After the last repetition, break the pattern with one short line that resolves it.
For epistrophe, end each line with the same word or phrase instead ('...for the farmer').
cards.before: The scheme helps farmers with faster credit, access to market prices and crop insurance.
cards.after: For the farmer who waits months for a loan, the money now comes before sowing. For the farmer who sells blind, the mandi price is now on her phone. For the farmer who loses a crop, the claim is now paid before the next one. That is what this scheme is for.
overuse_signs: Repetition runs in every section
Five or more repeated lines
Interchangeable lines that do not build
The repeated phrase is abstract ('We are committed to...')

cards.name: Descriptive anchor text (internal links)
cards.summary: The clickable words of a link name the destination, so readers, screen-reader users and search engines know what they will get before clicking. Good anchor text is a short noun phrase that matches the target page's topic.
use_for: internal links in blog posts, pillar pages and topic clusters
help-centre and knowledge base articles
newsletter and email links
website footers, menus and in-app links
avoid: 'Click here', 'read more', 'this', 'learn more' or a bare URL as the link: says nothing about the target and fails readers scanning a list of links; link the words that name the destination.
The same exact-match keyword as anchor on every page: reads as manipulation; vary naturally around the target's topic.
Whole sentences or paragraphs as one link: hard to scan and to tap; link the 2-6 words that name the target.
how: Write down what the target page is about in 2-6 words; usually its title or main keyword ('GST show-cause notice reply guide').
Rewrite the sentence so those words are the link; never put the link on 'click here', 'this' or 'read more'.
Check each link out of context: read only the linked words. Would a reader know where it goes? WCAG 2.4.4 asks that link purpose be clear from the link text or its context.
Different targets get different anchors; links with identical text on one page should go to the same place.
Say what is unusual about the target inside or right after the link: a file type and size, a login wall, an external site.
Keep links sparse: one link per target per section, placed where the reader would want to go next.
cards.before: We have updated our GST guide. Click [here] to read it.
cards.after: Before you reply, read our [guide to answering a GST show-cause notice].
overuse_signs: Every link on the site uses the same keyword phrase
Anchors longer than a line
So many links in a paragraph that it reads as blue text
The same page linked several times in one section

cards.name: Anecdote lead
cards.summary: Open with a short, true scene about one specific person at a moment of tension, then widen within a paragraph or two to the point the piece proves. Good anecdote leads are verified, brief and chosen because the person stands for the reader's problem.
use_for: feature articles and profile pieces
case studies (the client at the moment the problem hit)
long LinkedIn posts and newsletters
NGO fundraising appeals
policy or scheme explainers (one beneficiary before the numbers)
avoid: Invented or composite people presented as real: a credibility and legal risk; use real cases with consent, and say 'name changed' when you anonymise.
News, B2B emails and anything a busy reader skims: lead with the point instead (fw:inverted_pyramid, fw:bluf).
Stories about the brand or the founder when the reader came for their own problem: make the customer the character.
how: Find one real person whose experience shows the piece's point: an interview, a client file, a reader email. Get consent and check the details.
Start inside a specific moment: a place, a time, an action ('At 11 pm on filing day, Meena was still on the GST portal').
Add one detail only this person has: the object, the number, the exact words they said.
Keep it to 3-6 sentences with one tension; no backstory dump.
Bridge to the point with a nut graf: why this story matters and who else it stands for.
Come back to the person near the end to close the loop (tech:callback).
cards.before: Many small business owners in India struggle with GST compliance, which can lead to penalties.
cards.after: Meena Joshi runs a three-person saree business from her home in Jaipur. Last March a GST notice arrived for a return she was sure she had filed. She had clicked Save, not Submit. The notice gave her a month to reply. Her mistake is common, and it is fixable. Here is how.
overuse_signs: Every post opens with 'Meet X' or a timestamp
The story never connects to the point
Generic details that could belong to anyone
The anecdote runs longer than a third of a short piece before the point appears

cards.name: Answer-first paragraph
cards.summary: Under a heading phrased as the reader's question, the first one or two sentences give the direct answer (yes/no, the number, the definition, the main condition), and the rest adds steps, exceptions and evidence. A good answer-first paragraph is still correct when its first two sentences are lifted out alone.
use_for: FAQ pages and FAQ blocks
how-to and informational articles
knowledge base and help-centre articles
glossary entries
comparison articles where the reader asks 'which one?'
avoid: Selling it as a way to 'get cited by AI': Google says its AI features need no special optimisation beyond normal SEO; write it because it serves the reader.
Putting the key condition in paragraph three, so the lifted answer is wrong: move the main condition into sentence one or two.
Opinion pieces, stories and essays where the delay is the point: use a hook or an anecdote lead instead.
how: Phrase the heading as the question readers actually ask; take the wording from search queries, sales calls or support tickets.
Sentence one: the answer itself (yes / no / the number / the definition / the recommendation), with the main condition attached.
Sentence two: the most important qualifier or the next action.
Then expand: steps, exceptions, examples, sources.
Test: copy only the first two sentences into a blank note. Do they answer the question correctly on their own? If not, rewrite.
Do not restate the question or warm up ('Many people wonder whether...', 'Great question').
cards.before:
Can I change my flight booking?
Travel plans can change for many reasons, and at FlyEasy we understand how stressful that can be. That is why our flexible policies are designed with you in mind...
cards.after:
Can I change my flight booking?
Yes. You can change a FlyEasy booking in My Trips up to 2 hours before departure; you pay any fare difference, and Flex fares have no change fee. Here is how to do it on the app.
overuse_signs: Headings forced into questions nobody asks
Every paragraph of a narrative piece opens with a one-line verdict
The answer sentence repeats the heading word for word
Thin one-line answers with no expansion, written only to chase a snippet

cards.name: Antithesis
cards.summary: Set two genuinely opposed ideas side by side in balanced, parallel phrases so the contrast makes the point. Good antithesis contrasts two real, concrete things; the reflexive 'It's not X, it's Y' frame is a listed AI tell.
use_for: taglines and campaign lines
speech lines meant to be quoted
the closing line of a LinkedIn post or op-ed
positioning copy (the old way vs your way)
avoid: Reflexive 'It's not X, it's Y' / 'not just X, but Y': a listed AI tell that pcw.py check flags; state Y directly or contrast two concrete things.
Straw-man contrasts that pretend the reader or a rival believes X: readers notice; contrast real options.
Several antitheses in a row: it starts to sound like a speechwriter's template; one per short piece.
how: Name the two things that truly oppose each other: cost vs value, before vs after, short-term vs long-term, what they fear vs what happens.
Write both halves in matching grammar: same length, same word classes, same rhythm.
Put the idea you want remembered in the second half.
Cut every word that does not have a partner in the other half.
Check it is true: the contrast must describe a real difference the piece can back.
Ration it to one per short piece, ideally at the open or the close, and never in the 'not X, it's Y' frame.
cards.before: Our CA firm offers both affordable pricing and high-quality service.
cards.after: Fees a startup can afford. Filings a tax officer can't fault.
overuse_signs: More than one antithesis in 300 words
Contrast used to deny a claim nobody made
Mirrored halves with no concrete noun in either
The same frame opening several posts

sources.title: Antithesis (Wikipedia)

cards.name: Authority proof
cards.summary: Answer 'says who?' by citing a credential, a named expert, a certification, a publication or a data source, placed right where the reader is most likely to doubt. Good authority proof is specific, checkable and relevant to the exact claim it supports (Authority is one of Cialdini's principles of persuasion).
use_for: landing and sales pages, next to the boldest claim and the price
services pages for CA, legal, medical and finance practices
B2B case studies and white papers
one credibility line in a cold email
author bios on thought-leadership articles
avoid: Fake or inflated credentials, 'as seen on' logos without real coverage, or expert quotes you cannot source: misleading-advertising risk under codes such as ASCI's; use only what you can document.
Irrelevant authority (a cricketer endorsing a tax app): it borrows fame, not trust; match the authority to the doubt.
Credential dumps in the opening line of a cold email: give one line of proof after the reader's problem.
how: Mark the 2-3 sentences where a sceptical reader would ask 'says who?': the big promise, the price, the risky step.
Pick the proof that answers that doubt: a credential, a regulator's licence or registration, a named expert quote, a media mention, or data with its source.
Make it checkable: registration number, publication name and date, report title and year, the expert's full name and role.
Place it next to the claim it supports, not in a logo strip at the bottom of the page.
Keep it relevant: an ex-tax-department officer on the team proves more for a tax service than a celebrity does.
Before using endorsements, certifications, or health and finance claims, check the compliance cards (comp:asci_code; comp:ftc_endorsement_guides for US audiences).
cards.before: Our team has a lot of experience handling tax notices.
cards.after: Your reply is drafted by CA Ritu Sharma (ICAI member since 2011), who has answered more than 300 GST notices for D2C brands.
overuse_signs: Logo walls with no claim attached
'Experts say' in every paragraph
Titles and degrees listed before any benefit
'Award-winning' with no award named

sources.title: Cialdini: Seven Principles of Persuasion (Influence at Work)
sources.supports: Authority is one of the seven principles

cards.name: Match copy to awareness level
cards.summary: Before writing, decide how much the reader already knows (unaware, problem-aware, solution-aware, product-aware or most aware, the five levels from Eugene Schwartz's Breakthrough Advertising, 1966) and open the copy at that level. Done well, a cold reader meets their problem first and a warm reader meets the offer first.
use_for: choosing the opening of a sales page, ad or email
writing different ad copy for cold, warm and retargeting audiences
planning the order of an email sequence
briefing landing-page variants per traffic source
avoid: Opening with the product name for cold traffic: they have no reason to care yet; lead with the problem or a story.
Re-explaining the problem to a returning customer or a cart abandoner: they want the offer; go straight to it.
Treating the five levels as a rigid script: readers sit between levels; use the model to choose the opening, then write normally.
how: Identify where the reader comes from: a cold reel, a search for a problem, a search for your brand name, a retargeting list, your own customer list.

Assign one level: unaware (does not feel the problem), problem-aware (feels it, no solution in mind), solution-aware (knows solutions exist, not yours), product-aware (knows you, not convinced), most aware (wants it, needs the deal).

Open to match: unaware = a story or identity hook; problem-aware = name the pain in the reader's words; solution-aware = why your mechanism beats the alternatives; product-aware = proof, objections, guarantee; most aware = offer, price, deadline, button.
Expect length to shrink as awareness rises: the less the reader knows, the more you have to explain.
If traffic is mixed, write one variant per level instead of one page that opens everywhere.
cards.before: (retargeting ad to people who left a face oil in their cart) Struggling with dry winter skin? Discover the science of deep hydration and why most moisturisers fail...
cards.after: (same audience) Your kumkumadi night oil is still in the cart. Order by Sunday and shipping to Pune is free.
overuse_signs: The copy names the level to the reader ('If you're solution-aware...')
All five levels stuffed into one page
Long problem agitation in a retargeting ad
Every piece for the brand opens the same way regardless of channel

sources.title: Eugene Schwartz 5 levels of awareness explained (Selzee)
sources.supports: summary of the five levels from Breakthrough Advertising (1966) (secondary)

cards.name: Big idea
cards.summary: One fresh, simple central idea that organises the whole piece and makes the offer memorable and different (a term associated with David Ogilvy and direct-response copywriting). A good big idea fits in one sentence, belongs to this offer only, and every section of the piece serves it.
use_for: campaign and ad concepts
long-form sales letters and VSL scripts
brand manifestos and launch sequences
pitch decks and keynote talks
avoid: Feature lists posing as an idea ('fast, secure, easy'): nobody remembers them; find the one thing that is true only of this offer.
A clever idea the product cannot back: the proof must exist (tech:reason_why), or the idea becomes a broken promise.
Two or three ideas in one piece: split them into separate ads, emails or pages.
how: Gather raw material first: product facts, customer words (tech:voice_of_customer_mining), competitor claims, and what only this offer can say.
Write 10-20 candidate ideas, each one sentence that makes a claim, a promise or a new way to see the problem.
Test each: Is it new to this audience? Can a stranger repeat it after one read? Is it true and provable? Does it lead naturally to the offer?
Pick one and write it at the top of the draft.
Build the headline, lead, proof and CTA so each part advances that idea; cut any section that argues a second one.
Give the idea a handle the reader can carry: a name for the method, a metaphor, a single number.
cards.before: KhataPay is a fast, secure, easy UPI app with cashback, bill payments and investment options.
cards.after: Big idea: 'Your kirana's udhaar notebook, now on your phone.' Every ad in the launch shows a shopkeeper closing a month of credit accounts in one evening, without the notebook.
overuse_signs: The idea needs a paragraph to explain
It could be pasted onto a competitor's ad unchanged
Sections that never come back to it
A pun with no promise behind it

cards.name: Bold for skimmers
cards.summary: Bold a few short phrases that carry the meaning on their own, so a reader who sees only the bold still gets the gist. Good bolding is sparse and consistent; overused boldface is a listed sign of AI writing.
use_for: long blog posts, guides and ultimate guides
help-centre and knowledge base articles
internal memos and policy documents (dates, deadlines, actions)
email newsletters read on the move
avoid: Bolding whole sentences or every other line: nothing stands out and it reads as AI output; bold 3-8 word phrases only.
Faking bold with Unicode 'bold letters' on platforms without native bold: screen readers and search can stumble on them; check the platform card's formatting before relying on bold.
Mixing bold, italics, capitals and underline in one piece: pick one emphasis style; on the web keep underline for links.
how: Finish the draft first; add bold last.
For each section, pick the one phrase (3-8 words) a skimmer must not miss: the deadline, the number, the key term, the action.
Bold that phrase, not the sentence around it; put it early in the paragraph where you can.
Read only the bold text, top to bottom. It should summarise the piece; if it does not, change the selections.
Cap it at about one bold phrase per paragraph, with many paragraphs carrying none.
Do not bold keywords for SEO; bold is for the reader.
cards.before: **The new leave policy applies from 1 April and all employees must submit requests through the HR portal at least 7 days in advance, except for sick leave.**
cards.after: The new leave policy applies **from 1 April**. Apply in the HR portal **at least 7 days ahead**; sick leave is the only exception.
overuse_signs: Whole sentences in bold
Bold in nearly every paragraph
Bolded label plus colon at the start of every bullet
Bold, italics and capitals used together for emphasis

sources.title: NN/g: Formatting long-form content
sources.supports: bolding and formatting to support scanning

sources.title: Wikipedia: Signs of AI writing
sources.supports: overuse of boldface is a listed AI tell

cards.name: Bucket brigades
cards.summary: A short conversational phrase at the end of one paragraph or the start of the next ('The catch?', 'It gets worse.', 'So what changed?') that carries the reader across the break. Good bucket brigades are rare, specific to what follows and paid off at once; several stock ones overlap with AI tells.
use_for: long blog posts and sales pages
email newsletters
video, reel and YouTube voice-over transitions ('Ab twist suniye.')
LinkedIn posts where the reader decides at every line break
avoid: Stock bridges ('Here's the thing', 'Real talk', 'Let that sink in', 'But wait, there's more'): read as formula or AI, and pcw.py check flags some; write a bridge specific to the next point.
One at every paragraph break: the rhythm turns into a tic; use 2-4 in a long piece.
Bridges that promise more than the next paragraph delivers: readers feel tricked; pay off in the very next line.
how: Find the drop-off points: after a long paragraph, before a list, before the proof, before the price.
Write a 2-5 word bridge that points at the specific content coming next ('So why did 36 fail?' beats 'But wait').
Put it on its own line, or as the last sentence of the paragraph before the break.
Make the next line pay it off immediately.
Use 2-4 in a long piece, never two in a row, and never the same one twice.
In Hinglish scripts use natural spoken bridges ('Par yahin galti hoti hai.', 'Ab asli baat.') and avoid translated English stock phrases.
cards.before: We tested 40 face serums over three months. Most of them did not deliver the results claimed on the label. Only four improved hydration readings in our tests.
cards.after:
We tested 40 face serums over three months.

The result?

36 did not do what the label promised. Four did, and the best of them costs Rs 349.
overuse_signs: A bridge at every paragraph break
The same phrase used twice
Lines that pcw.py check flags as fake-candid openers ('Here's the thing', 'Real talk')
A bridge followed by a weak or delayed payoff

sources.title: Copyhackers: How to engage with the bucket brigade technique

sources.title: Backlinko: Copywriting, 7 fundamentals
sources.supports: Brian Dean's use of bucket brigades in blog posts

cards.name: Bulleted and numbered lists
cards.summary: Turn a run of three or more parallel items into a list: numbered when order matters (steps, rankings), bulleted when it does not. A good list has a lead-in sentence, items in the same grammatical form, and items short enough to scan.
use_for: how-to steps and instructions (numbered)
feature and benefit lists on product and landing pages
eligibility, requirement and document checklists
action items in emails and memos
knowledge base articles
avoid: Bullets for an argument or a story: lists strip out the 'because' and 'so' that connect reasoning; keep reasoning in prose.
Turning every section into bullets: reads like slides or AI output; mix prose and lists.
Assuming list markdown renders everywhere: Instagram captions, WhatsApp and SMS need manual line breaks with numerals or a symbol; check the platform card's formatting.
how: Find sentences that string together three or more items, or that describe a sequence.
Choose the type: numbered for steps in order or a stated count; bulleted for items with no order.
Write a lead-in that says what the list is ('To claim the refund, upload:').
Make every item the same form: all start with a verb, or all are noun phrases, or all are full sentences; punctuate them the same way.
In a bulleted list put the most important item first.
Keep one idea per item; if an item needs a paragraph, it is a subsection, not a bullet.
Two items are a sentence, not a list.
cards.before: To apply, you will need your PAN card, and also a cancelled cheque should be attached, and you must also upload your bank statements for the last 6 months and then finally sign the form.
cards.after:
To apply, upload:
- your PAN card
- a cancelled cheque
- bank statements for the last 6 months
- the signed application form
overuse_signs: More than half the piece is bullets
Nested bullets three levels deep
One- or two-item lists
A bold label and colon opening every bullet

sources.supports: when to use numbered vs bulleted lists

cards.name: But / therefore links
cards.summary: Join story beats with 'but' (a complication) or 'therefore' (a consequence), never 'and then', so each event causes the next. The rule comes from South Park creators Trey Parker and Matt Stone's advice to an NYU class; a good outline reads as a chain of causes, not a list of events.
use_for: brand and founder stories
case studies (problem, setback, response, result)
reel, Short and ad scripts with a story arc
micro-drama and web-series episodes
narrative explainers and video essays
avoid: Expository content (how-to steps, specs, FAQs): sequence is the point there; use numbered steps, not a causal story.
Forcing a 'but' where nothing went wrong: invented setbacks in a case study are misleading; use the real complications.
Leaving the literal words 'but' and 'so' at the start of every sentence: the rule tests the outline; vary the connectors in the final draft.
how: Write the story as a list of beats, one sentence each.
Read the joint between every pair of beats aloud with 'and then'. Wherever 'and then' fits, the beats are only in sequence, not connected.
Rewrite each joint so it takes 'but' (something goes wrong, a new obstacle appears) or 'therefore / so' (the character acts because of the previous beat).
Cut any beat that cannot be linked either way; it is not part of this story.
Alternate: a run of 'therefores' with no 'but' has no tension; a run of 'buts' with no 'therefore' leaves the character with no agency.
In the final draft the words themselves are optional; the causal chain must survive.
cards.before: Riya started a pickle brand in Indore. And then she listed on Amazon. And then she got her first 100 orders. And then she launched a mango range.
cards.after: Riya started a pickle brand in Indore, but her first 200 jars leaked in transit. So she moved to glass jars with a wax seal, but courier costs doubled. So she stopped shipping nationally and sold only in Madhya Pradesh, where customers reordered every month and kept asking for one thing: a mango range.
overuse_signs: Every sentence starts with 'But' or 'So'
Setbacks manufactured to make the arc look dramatic
So many reversals that the point is lost
Causal story forced onto a piece the reader wanted as steps

sources.title: Aerogramme Studio: Writing advice from South Park's Trey Parker and Matt Stone
sources.supports: the 'but/therefore' rule from their NYU class visit

sources.title: Writing Advice from Matt Stone & Trey Parker @ NYU (video)

cards.name: Front-loaded button labels
cards.summary: Label buttons and commands with a short, specific verb phrase that says what happens on tap ('Save draft', 'Pay Rs 499', 'Delete folder'), not 'OK', 'Submit' or 'Yes'. NN/g's guidance: lead with the verb, use 2-4 words, be specific rather than cutesy, and use the same label for the same action everywhere.
use_for: app and website buttons
checkout, payment and form submit buttons
dialog and confirmation actions
CTA buttons in emails and landing pages
quick-reply buttons in WhatsApp Business templates (check the platform card for limits)
avoid: Generic labels (OK, Submit, Yes / No, Click here): the user must read the surrounding text to know what happens; name the action.
Cute or branded labels ('Let's goooo!', 'Make magic'): unclear and grating on repeat; keep brand voice for headings and empty states.
Different labels for the same action on different screens ('Save', 'Store', 'Keep'): users wonder whether they differ; pick one (tech:consistent_terminology).
how: Write what happens after the tap as a full sentence ('This sends the invoice to the client').
Cut it to verb + object, 2-4 words, verb first, no articles ('Send invoice').
Add the one detail that changes the decision when it fits: price, count or destination ('Pay Rs 499', 'Continue to payment').
Label the state the tap will produce, not the current one (a playing video shows 'Pause').
Use the identical label for the same action in the UI, emails, notifications and help articles.
Add an ellipsis only when the command asks for more input ('Export...'); give icon-only buttons a tooltip.
In Hindi UI keep labels as short and fix one imperative form for the whole product ('karein' or 'karo', never both).
cards.before: Checkout screen buttons: [Submit]  [Cancel]
cards.after: Checkout screen buttons: [Pay Rs 499]  [Back to cart]
overuse_signs: Labels longer than four words
Every button starts with 'Get' or 'Start'
ALL CAPS on every button
'My' and 'your' mixed in the same flow ('My orders' next to 'Your cart')

sources.title: NN/g: UI Copy, guidelines for command names
sources.supports: command labels should be specific and start with the important word; 2-4 words, lead with verbs, replace OK with the explicit action, keep labels consistent (checked 2026-10-04)

cards.name: Callback
cards.summary: Bring back an earlier line, image, detail or joke near the end, so the piece feels closed and the reader is rewarded for paying attention. A good callback means something new when it returns: the same detail lands differently because of what happened in between.
use_for: closing a feature, essay or LinkedIn post by returning to the opening scene
stand-up sets and sketch comedy
wedding speeches, toasts and keynotes
reel and ad scripts that end where they began
newsletter sign-offs that pick up the opening line
avoid: A callback to something the audience barely noticed: it confuses instead of rewarding; make the first mention vivid.
Explaining the callback ('Remember the trunk I mentioned earlier?'): it kills the effect; just bring the detail back.
A callback in place of the CTA in selling copy: put the callback first, then the ask.
how: Plant it early: a specific, memorable detail (an object, a phrase, a number, a joke) in the first fifth of the piece.
Make the plant work on its own; it must not look like a setup.
Let the middle change its context: what was learned, what went wrong, what got solved.
Near the end, bring the detail back in nearly the same words, now carrying a new meaning.
Put it in the last line or two and do not explain it.
Use one main callback in a short piece; in comedy several are fine, but each needs its own plant.
cards.before: Opening: 'My father has kept every electricity bill since 1998 in a steel trunk.' Ending: 'That is why I built a bill-tracking app.'
cards.after: Opening: 'My father has kept every electricity bill since 1998 in a steel trunk.' Ending: 'Last week he opened the app, scrolled back to 1998, and asked me where he should put the trunk.'
overuse_signs: Three or more callbacks in a short piece
The plant is obviously a setup
The returning detail means exactly what it meant before
A callback to an inside joke the reader never saw

sources.title: Callback (comedy) (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: a joke referring back to an earlier one

cards.name: Captions and subtitle writing
cards.summary: Write on-video captions as short lines broken at natural phrase boundaries and timed so they can be read comfortably, condensing the words when speech is fast. Netflix's English (USA) timed-text guide sets 42 characters per line, two lines maximum and up to 20 characters per second for adult programmes (17 for children's); BBC guidance also recommends two lines maximum for landscape and square video.
use_for: burned-in captions on reels, Shorts and YouTube videos
subtitles for brand films, documentaries and interviews
Hindi-to-English and English-to-Hindi subtitle files
accessibility captions for webinars and course videos
avoid: Verbatim transcripts of fast speech: unreadable at speed; condense to the reading-speed limit and keep the meaning.
Captions over faces, lower-thirds or the platform's buttons: viewers miss both; place them in the safe area and check the platform card.
Paraphrasing so freely that the caption contradicts the speaker, or changes a quote: condense, never rewrite the claim.
how: Start from an accurate transcript; fix names, numbers and brand terms before anything else.
Split into caption events at sentence or clause boundaries, one thought per event.
Hold each event to two lines and to your spec's line length (Netflix English: 42 characters); vertical reels usually need shorter lines than that because the frame is narrow.
Break lines after punctuation or before a conjunction or preposition; never split an article from its noun, an adjective from its noun, a first name from a surname, or a pronoun from its verb.
Check reading speed against your spec (Netflix adult: 20 characters per second). If an event is too fast, cut fillers, repetition and false starts instead of shortening its time on screen.
Keep captions in sync: a punchline or a number must not appear before it is spoken.
For Hinglish speech pick one script (Roman or Devanagari) per video and spell recurring words the same way throughout.
cards.before:
[1] So what we decided to do was basically the
    GST filing for all of our sellers on the
[2] platform from April.
overuse_signs: Three or more lines on screen
Every word popping in a different colour on a long explainer
Emoji in every caption
Captions so condensed that names, numbers or quotes change

sources.title: BBC Subtitle Guidelines
sources.supports: line-break, timing and length guidance; two lines maximum recommended for landscape/square video

sources.title: Netflix English (USA) Timed Text Style Guide
sources.supports: 42 characters per line; maximum two lines; reading speed up to 20 characters per second (adult) and 17 (children's); line-break rules (checked 2026-10-04)

cards.name: Character with a want
cards.summary: Give the person at the centre of the story a clear, concrete desire and something in the way, so the reader has someone to root for. In brand stories that person is the customer; the brand is the help, not the hero.
use_for: brand stories and case studies
ad scripts, TVCs and UGC ad scripts
reel, Short and micro-drama scripts
fundraising appeals
founder stories told from one decisive moment
avoid: Abstract wants ('to be happy', 'to grow the business'): nobody can picture them; make the want concrete, with an object and a deadline.
The brand as the character who wants something ('We set out to revolutionise...'): readers root for people like them; cast the customer and make the brand the guide (fw:storybrand_sb7).
A want with no obstacle: there is no story; add the real obstacle (tech:conflict_and_stakes).
how: Choose one specific person: the customer, the beneficiary, the founder on one particular day. Never 'users' or 'people'.
Write the want as one sentence with a concrete object and, where possible, a deadline ('Anjali needs her daughter's school fee paid by Monday').
Name what stands in the way: money, time, a system, another person, or the character's own fear.
Show the character acting on the want within the first few lines.
Bring the product or service in as the help that changes the odds, after the reader cares.
End when the want is met, refused or changed, and make clear which.
cards.before: At SwiftLoans, we are passionate about empowering customers with fast, hassle-free personal loans.
cards.after: Anjali needs Rs 48,000 for her daughter's school fee by Monday. The bank wants three months of salary slips; she has been freelancing for two. SwiftLoans looked at her invoices instead and paid on Friday.
overuse_signs: Every piece opens 'Meet X, who wanted...'
The want changes mid-piece for no reason
Obstacles that dissolve with no effort
The product appears before the reader cares about the person

sources.title: Protagonist (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: the protagonist as the character whose goals drive the story

sources.title: Character arc (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: change a character undergoes in pursuing a goal

cards.name: Chiasmus
cards.summary: Reverse the order of two key words in a second clause (A-B, then B-A) to make a line that sticks and gets quoted. Good chiasmus is true in both halves; the reversal adds meaning, not just symmetry.
use_for: taglines and campaign lines
speech closers
op-ed headlines and last lines
the final line of a LinkedIn post
avoid: A reversal whose second half is empty or false ('We don't sell to live, we live to sell'): it sounds clever and says nothing; test the claim.
Echoing a famous chiasmus: it reads as borrowed; build the line from the client's own terms.
More than one per piece: the point is one line people remember.
how: Find two key terms that relate in both directions: shops/customers, time/money, work/life, city/people.
Write the first clause with A before B.
Write the second clause with B before A, in the same grammar.
Check that both halves are true for this offer or argument.
Cut to the shortest version that still reads naturally aloud.
Place it at the open or the close, once.
cards.before: Shops that do not adapt to how customers buy today will lose those customers.
cards.after: Shops that don't change with their customers soon have customers who change shops.
overuse_signs: The line needs a second read to parse
Both halves say the same thing
Used mid-body instead of at the open or close
The same pattern across many posts for one brand

sources.title: Chiasmus (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: definition of the device

cards.name: Chunking
cards.summary: Break content into small, labelled groups (short paragraphs, lists, sections under headings) so the reader can process it and find what they need (NN/g). Good chunking groups by meaning, in the order the reader needs it, not by a fixed length.
use_for: web pages, landing pages and help articles
scheme and policy explainers
emails with several asks or several pieces of information
onboarding flows and carousels
long reports with an executive reader
avoid: Chopping by length instead of meaning (a break every three lines regardless of topic): readers lose the thread; break where the idea changes.
Tiny chunks with a heading for every sentence: navigation overhead; merge related ones.
Essays, op-eds and narrative pieces: heavy chunking breaks the argument; use paragraphing and transitions instead.
how: List every piece of information the reader needs.
Group related items; each group answers one question or covers one task.
Give each group a label: a heading or a lead phrase that names it (tech:descriptive_subheads).
Order the groups in the reader's sequence: what they need to know or do first comes first.
Inside each group keep paragraphs short and use a list for parallel items.
Separate groups with white space.
Chunk long numbers the way people read them aloud (mobile numbers as 98290 12345).
cards.before: The scholarship is open to students in classes 9 to 12 whose family income is below Rs 2.5 lakh and you need to upload your marksheet, income certificate and Aadhaar on the portal before 31 October, after which your school will verify the application.
cards.after:
Who can apply: students in classes 9-12 with family income below Rs 2.5 lakh.
What to upload: marksheet, income certificate, Aadhaar.
Last date: 31 October.
What happens next: your school verifies the application.
overuse_signs: A heading every two sentences
Every sentence its own paragraph in an essay
Lists nested inside lists
Carousel slides with one word each

sources.title: NN/g: How Chunking Helps Content Processing
sources.supports: definition and methods

cards.name: Cliffhanger
cards.summary: End a section, email, episode or slide at an unresolved moment, so the reader comes back for the next part. A good cliffhanger raises one specific question, says when the answer arrives, and the next part pays it off at once.
use_for: email and launch sequences
serialized fiction, web-series and micro-drama episodes
multi-part reel and YouTube series
X threads and carousels (slide to slide)
newsletters that run a story across issues
avoid: Standalone pieces (a single blog post, a one-off ad): there is no next part; resolve inside the piece.
Teasing a payoff the next part does not deliver: readers unsubscribe; plan both parts before publishing the first.
Holding back information the reader needs to act (a deadline, a price, a safety step): give the practical facts now and hold back only the story.
how: Decide the next part's payoff first: the reveal, the result or the decision.
End the current part just before it, at a moment of tension or a choice.
State the open question concretely, not vaguely ('what clause 14 said', not 'something shocking').
Tell the reader when and where the answer comes: tomorrow's email, Part 2 at 7 pm, the next slide.
Open the next part by answering the question in its first lines; do not re-tease.
Resolve every cliffhanger you open.
cards.before: That's all for today. Thanks for reading, see you in the next email!
cards.after: Rahul signed the shop lease on Friday. On Monday his CA read clause 14 and went quiet. Tomorrow's email: what clause 14 said, and the one line that would have saved him Rs 4 lakh.
overuse_signs: Every email or episode ends on a tease
The next part opens with a recap and another tease
The cliffhanger replaces the CTA
'You won't believe what happened next' style vagueness

sources.title: Cliffhanger (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: definition of the device

cards.name: Concrete nouns and strong verbs
cards.summary: Use nouns a reader can picture and verbs that carry the action, instead of abstract nouns, weak verbs (make, do, have, be) and stacked adjectives (Strunk's rule 12: use definite, specific, concrete language). Good concrete copy lets the reader see who did what to what.
use_for: product descriptions and ad copy
case studies and testimonials
news, features and speeches
revising AI drafts full of abstractions
avoid: Inflated verbs (utilise, leverage, facilitate, elevate): weaker than the plain verb, and some are listed AI tells; use the plain verb.
Inventing numbers or details to sound concrete: a made-up figure is a false claim; use real data or a real example.
Purple prose: vivid verbs and images in every line of business copy distract; one concrete detail per point is enough.
how: Circle abstract nouns, especially nominalisations ending in -tion, -ment, -ance, -ity ('implementation', 'enhancement').
Turn each back into a verb where you can ('carry out the implementation of' becomes 'implement'; see tech:unhide_verbs).
Replace weak verb + noun pairs with one strong verb ('make a decision' becomes 'decide', 'give assistance' becomes 'help').
Replace category nouns with the specific thing the reader knows ('stationery' becomes 'notebooks and gel pens', 'retail establishment' becomes 'kirana').
Delete adjectives and adverbs that a stronger noun or verb makes redundant ('walked slowly' becomes 'shuffled').
Re-read each sentence: can you picture it? If not, add one real, concrete detail.
cards.before: Our solution facilitates the enhancement of operational efficiency for retail establishments.
cards.after: Our app cuts a kirana owner's evening stock count from an hour to ten minutes.
overuse_signs: Every verb is dramatic (slashes, skyrockets, crushes)
Thesaurus words in plain contexts
Sensory detail in a compliance notice or terms page
Concrete-sounding details that are made up

sources.title: Strunk, The Elements of Style (1920 ed., public domain, Project Gutenberg)
sources.supports: rule 12: use definite, specific, concrete language (checked against the Gutenberg text 2026-10-04)

sources.title: Nominalization (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: abstract nouns made from verbs weaken prose

cards.name: Confirmation-dialog copy
cards.summary: Ask for confirmation only before actions with serious consequences (destroying work, spending money, anything that cannot be undone), state the specific consequence, and label the buttons with the actions ('Delete file' / 'Keep file'), not Yes / No. NN/g warns that confirming routine actions trains users to click through without reading.
use_for: delete, cancel-subscription and close-account flows
payments and bulk sends ('Send to 4,200 contacts')
publish and irreversible settings changes in SaaS and admin consoles
app flows where a mistap costs the user money or data
avoid: Confirming routine actions (save, archive, close a tab): users stop reading and the dialog stops protecting them; offer an undo instead.
Generic 'Are you sure?' with Yes / No or OK / Cancel: the user has to reread to know which button deletes; name the actions on the buttons.

Guilt or fear wording on the decline option to stop cancellations ('No, I don't care about my savings'): confirm shaming is a listed dark pattern under India's 2023 guidelines (comp:ccpa_dark_patterns_2023); keep both options neutral.
how: Decide whether a dialog is needed at all: is the action destructive, costly or irreversible? If it can be undone, skip the dialog and show an undo ('Invoice deleted. Undo').
Title: the action as a short question naming the object ('Delete folder Q3 invoices?').
Body: the consequence in one or two sentences with identifying details (what is lost, how many, for whom, whether it can be recovered).
Primary button: the action itself ('Delete folder'). Secondary: the safe choice in plain words ('Keep folder').
For very dangerous actions, require a non-standard step such as typing the item's name.
Put secondary detail behind a 'Learn more' link rather than lengthening the body.
cards.before:
Are you sure?
[Yes]  [No]
cards.after:
Delete folder Q3 invoices?
All 214 invoices in it will be deleted for everyone on your team. You can't undo this.
[Delete folder]  [Keep folder]
overuse_signs: A dialog after every action
'Are you sure?' as the title
A 'Cancel' button in a cancel-subscription dialog, so nobody knows what it cancels
Two confirmations in a row for a minor action

sources.title: NN/g: Confirmation Dialogs Can Prevent User Errors (If Not Overused)
sources.supports: when to use confirmation dialogs and how to word them; specific consequence, action-named buttons instead of Yes/No, undo as alternative, nonstandard action for dangerous operations (checked 2026-10-04)

sources.title: Gazette of India (30 Nov 2023): Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, 2023
sources.supports: confirm shaming listed among specified dark patterns (per the PCW compliance harvest)

cards.name: Conflict and stakes
cards.summary: Give the story an obstacle and make clear, early, what is lost if the character fails, so the reader cares how it ends. Good stakes are concrete (money, a date, a relationship, a reputation) and true, never inflated.
use_for: case studies and brand stories
ad scripts, reels and micro-dramas
fundraising appeals
speeches and talks
sales letters (the cost of doing nothing)
avoid: Inflated or invented stakes in case studies and testimonials: a misleading claim; use the client's real numbers with consent.
Abstract stakes ('the future of the business'): make them concrete with an amount, a date or a person.
Fear-heavy stakes aimed at vulnerable readers (health, debt, exams) in ads: manipulative and a compliance risk (comp:asci_code); state the risk calmly next to the solution.
how: Start from the want (tech:character_with_a_want).
Name the obstacle: a person, a system, nature, time, or the character's own fear or habit.
Spell out the stakes as a concrete loss: if X does not happen by Y, Z is gone ('If the order misses Diwali week, the year's profit goes with it').
Raise them once in the middle: the obstacle grows or the deadline moves closer.
Resolve: show how the obstacle was beaten, or not, and what it cost.
In business copy check every stake against the facts before publishing.
cards.before: Sharma Sweets wanted to sell online, so they partnered with us and now their business is doing great.
cards.after: Sharma Sweets earns most of its year in the three weeks before Diwali. Last year, on 1 October, their courier partner shut down. They had 1,800 pre-orders and no way to ship them. We had a new partner picking up from their Lucknow kitchen in four days; 1,760 boxes arrived before Diwali.
overuse_signs: Every story is life or death
Stakes raised and never resolved
A villain made of the customer's family or a competitor
High drama for a product that fixes a minor convenience

sources.title: Conflict (narrative) (Wikipedia)
sources.supports: conflict as the engine of narrative

cards.name: Consistent terminology
cards.summary: Call one thing by one name everywhere (UI, help articles, emails, ads) and keep a word list so writers do not swap terms for style. NN/g's consistency heuristic says users should not have to wonder whether different words mean the same thing, and 'elegant variation' (synonym swapping) is a listed sign of AI writing.
use_for: UX microcopy and onboarding flows
help centres, product docs and API docs
legal, policy and terms documents
content programmes with several writers
bilingual Hindi-English products
avoid: Swapping synonyms to avoid repetition (invoice / bill / statement): readers assume they are different things; repeat the term.
Internal or engineering names in user-facing copy (SKU, tenant, workspace entity): use the user's word, then keep it.
Forcing one name on two things that really differ: different features need different names.
how: Start a term list (style sheet): each key noun and action, the chosen term, and the banned variants ('Wallet': not balance, account, e-purse).
Choose the words users already use, taken from support tickets, search queries and reviews, not internal jargon.
Use the exact term in buttons, headings, help articles, emails and notifications, with the same capitalisation.
In long-form copy, resist synonyms for the same thing: if paragraph one says 'invoice', paragraph four does not say 'bill'.
For Hindi or bilingual products, fix the Hindi term too and decide once whether to translate or transliterate ('Wallet' as 'वॉलेट' or 'बटुआ', never both).
Before publishing, search the draft for every banned variant.
cards.before: Add money to your Wallet. ... Your balance is running low. ... Top up your e-purse to keep ordering.
cards.after: Add money to your Wallet. ... Your Wallet is running low. ... Add money to your Wallet to keep ordering.
overuse_signs: The term repeated so often in a short message that it reads robotic; use 'it' where nothing is ambiguous
Every product term capitalised
Plain everyday words banned in favour of a brand term users do not know
A term list so long nobody checks it

sources.title: NN/g: Consistency and Standards (usability heuristic #4)
sources.supports: users should not wonder whether different words mean the same thing

sources.title: Wikipedia: Signs of AI writing
sources.supports: elegant variation (swapping synonyms for the same thing) is a listed tell
